claims.evidence: This is a general principle supported by citations.

claims.claim: X-ray crystallography, NMR, and cryo-electron microscopy mainly provide static snapshots of highly-populated conformational states.
claims.source: Biophysical techniques such as X-ray crystallography (Shi, 2014), nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) (Huang and Kalodimos, 2017), and cryo-electron microscopy (Fernandez-Leiro and Scheres, 2016) mainly provide static snapshots of highly-populated conformational states.
claims.evidence: This describes limitations of experimental techniques, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Molecular simulations provide atomistic detail and insight into relevant conformational transitions.
claims.source: By contrast, molecular simulations provide atomistic detail---a prerequisite to structure-guided rational ligand design---and insight into relevant conformational transitions (Wei et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This describes advantages of computational approaches, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Markov state models have shown the power of distributed molecular simulations in resolving complex kinetic landscapes of proteins.
claims.source: The emergence of Markov state models (MSMs) has shown the power of distributed molecular simulations in resolving complex kinetic landscapes of proteins (Husic and Pande, 2018; Plattner et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of MSMs, supported by citations.

claims.claim: MSMs have been used to identify key intermediates for enzyme activation and allosteric modulation.
claims.source: Recently, MSMs have been used to identify key intermediates for enzyme activation (Shukla et al., 2014; Sultan et al., 2017) and allosteric modulation (Bowman et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This describes prior applications of MSMs, supported by citations.

claims.claim: MSM approaches are limited by the number of seed structures and timescales accessible by molecular simulations relative to complicated conformational transitions.
claims.source: However, these approaches are limited by the number of seed structures and timescales accessible by molecular simulations (generally microseconds for one structure) relative to the reality of complicated conformational transitions (up to milliseconds for multiple structures) (Klepeis et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This describes limitations of MSM approaches, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Efforts have been made to combine simulation with experiment to characterize conformational landscape models of proteins.
claims.source: To overcome the limitations of individual techniques, efforts have been made to combine simulation with experiment to characterize and experimentally validate conformational landscape models of proteins that provide insight into functions (Hart et al., 2016; Knoverek et al., 2019; Latallo et al., 2017; Zimmerman et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This describes prior integrative approaches, supported by citations.

claims.claim: PKMTs transfer a methyl group from the cofactor S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM).
claims.source: Protein lysine methyltransferases (PKMTs) comprise a subfamily of posttranslational modifying enzymes that transfer a methyl group from the cofactor S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) (Luo, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a basic biochemical fact about PKMTs, supported by citation.

claims.claim: PKMTs play epigenetic roles in gene transcription, cellular pluripotency, and organ development.
claims.source: PKMTs play epigenetic roles in gene transcription, cellular pluripotency, and organ development (Allis and Jenuwein, 2016; Murn and Shi, 2017).
claims.evidence: This describes biological functions of PKMTs, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Dysregulation of PKMTs has been implicated in neurological disorders and cancers.
claims.source: Their dysregulation has been implicated in neurological disorders and cancers (Dawson, 2017; Flavahan et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This describes disease associations of PKMTs, supported by citations.

claims.claim: SETD8 is the sole PKMT annotated for monomethylation of histone H4 lysine 20 (H4K20me).
claims.source: SETD8 (SET8/Pr-SET7/KMT5A) is the sole PKMT annotated for monomethylation of histone H4 lysine 20 (H4K20me) (Fang et al., 2002; Nishioka et al., 2002) and many nonhistone targets such as the tumor suppressor p53 and the p53-stabilizing factor Numb (Dhami et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is a specific fact about SETD8, supported by citations.

claims.claim: SETD8 methylates nonhistone targets such as the tumor suppressor p53 and the p53-stabilizing factor Numb.
claims.source: SETD8 (SET8/Pr-SET7/KMT5A) is the sole PKMT annotated for monomethylation of histone H4 lysine 20 (H4K20me) (Fang et al., 2002; Nishioka et al., 2002) and many nonhistone targets such as the tumor suppressor p53 and the p53-stabilizing factor Numb (Dhami et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This describes additional substrates of SETD8, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Disruption of endogenous SETD8 leads to cell cycle arrest and chromatin decondensation.
claims.source: Disruption of endogenous SETD8 leads to cell cycle arrest and chromatin decondensation, consistent with essential roles for SETD8 in transcriptional regulation and DNA damage response (Beck et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2010; Veschi et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This describes cellular consequences of SETD8 disruption, supported by citations.

claims.claim: SETD8 has been implicated in cancer invasiveness and metastasis.
claims.source: SETD8 has also been implicated in cancer invasiveness and metastasis (Yang et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This describes a disease association of SETD8, supported by citation.

claims.claim: High expression of SETD8 is associated with pediatric leukemia and its overall low survival rate.
claims.source: High expression of SETD8 is associated with pediatric leukemia and its overall low survival rate (Hashemi et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This describes a clinical association of SETD8, supported by citation.

claims.claim: It has been challenging to develop potent, selective, and cellularly active SETD8 inhibitors.
claims.source: While there is enormous interest in elucidating functional roles of SETD8 in disease, it has been challenging to develop potent, selective, and cellularly active SETD8 inhibitors (Blum et al., 2014; Milite et al., 2016a; Milite et al., 2016b).
claims.evidence: This describes a challenge in the field, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Four distinct crystal structures of SETD8 in alternative ligand-binding states were solved with covalent SETD8 inhibitors and native ligands.
claims.source: Here we solved four distinct crystal structures of SETD8 in alternative ligand-binding states with covalent SETD8 inhibitors and native ligands.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results.

claims.claim: An aggregate of six milliseconds of unbiased explicit solvent MD simulation data was generated for apo- and SAM-bound SETD8.
claims.source: With the aid of these new structures, we generated an aggregate of six milliseconds of unbiased explicit solvent MD simulation data for apo- and SAM-bound SETD8.
claims.evidence: This describes the computational work performed.

claims.claim: Apo-SETD8 conformers were clustered into 24 kinetically distinct, likely functionally relevant metastable conformational states.
claims.source: Using a machine learning approach to select features and hyperparameters for MSMs via extensive cross-validation, we clustered apo-SETD8 conformers into 24 kinetically distinct, likely functionally relevant metastable conformational states and annotated how the conformational landscape is remodeled upon SAM binding.
claims.evidence: This is a key result from the computational analysis.

claims.claim: The conformational landscape is remodeled upon SAM binding.
claims.source: Using a machine learning approach to select features and hyperparameters for MSMs via extensive cross-validation, we clustered apo-SETD8 conformers into 24 kinetically distinct, likely functionally relevant metastable conformational states and annotated how the conformational landscape is remodeled upon SAM binding.
claims.evidence: This is a key finding about the effect of SAM binding.

claims.claim: The conformational landscapes were explored experimentally with stopped-flow kinetics and isothermal titration calorimetry.
claims.source: We then explored these conformational landscape models experimentally with stopped-flow kinetics and isothermal titration calorimetry by examining SAM binding, characterizing rationally-designed SETD8 variants with increased catalytic efficiency, and resolving multiple timescales associated with transitions among these conformers.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental validation approaches used.

claims.claim: Rationally-designed SETD8 variants with increased catalytic efficiency were characterized.
claims.source: We then explored these conformational landscape models experimentally with stopped-flow kinetics and isothermal titration calorimetry by examining SAM binding, characterizing rationally-designed SETD8 variants with increased catalytic efficiency, and resolving multiple timescales associated with transitions among these conformers.
claims.evidence: This describes experimental validation of predictions from the model.

claims.claim: Multiple timescales associated with transitions among conformers were resolved.
claims.source: We then explored these conformational landscape models experimentally with stopped-flow kinetics and isothermal titration calorimetry by examining SAM binding, characterizing rationally-designed SETD8 variants with increased catalytic efficiency, and resolving multiple timescales associated with transitions among these conformers.
claims.evidence: This describes kinetic findings from experimental validation.

claims.claim: Cancer-associated SETD8 mutants alter the catalytic process allosterically through reshaping the conformational landscape rather than directly affecting the catalytic site.
claims.source: The resulting model furnishes key insights into how these dynamic conformations play a role in catalysis of SETD8 and how cancer-associated SETD8 mutants alter this process allosterically through reshaping the conformational landscape rather than directly affecting the catalytic site.
claims.evidence: This is a key mechanistic insight from the study.

claims.claim: MS4138 (Inh1) and SGSS05NS (Inh2) are two structurally distinct covalent inhibitors with desired potency against SETD8.
claims.source: Upon further optimization of these scaffolds, we identified MS4138 (Inh1) and SGSS05NS (Inh2) (Luo et al., 2015), two structurally distinct covalent inhibitors with the desired potency against SETD8 (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the inhibitors used in the study, with reference to figures showing their structures and potency.

claims.claim: X-ray crystal structures of SETD8 were solved in complex with Inh1 and Inh2.
claims.source: X-ray crystal structures of SETD8 were then solved in complex with Inh1 and Inh2, respectively (Figure 1b,c, Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3, Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results with reference to figures and table.

claims.claim: The Inh1- and Inh2-SETD8 binary complexes differ from the SETD8-SAH-H4 ternary complex by the distinct conformations of their post-SET motifs.
claims.source: Notably, despite the overall structural similarity of the pre-SET, SET, and SET-I motifs, the Inh1- and Inh2-SETD8 binary complexes (BC-Inh1 and BC-Inh2) differ from the SETD8-SAH-H4 ternary complex (TC) (Couture et al., 2005; Couture et al., 2008; Xiao et al., 2005) by the distinct conformations of their post-SET motifs.
claims.evidence: This is a structural comparison based on crystallographic data.

claims.claim: The post-SET motif of TC is characterized by its U-shaped topology with a double-kinked loop-helix-helix architecture.
claims.source: The post-SET motif of TC was characterized by its U-shaped topology with a double-kinked loop-helix-helix architecture, which appears to be optimally oriented for binding both SAM and a peptide substrate (Figures 1c and 2) (Couture et al., 2005; Couture et al., 2008; Xiao et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This describes a structural feature of the ternary complex, supported by citations and figures.

claims.claim: BC-Inh1 and BC-Inh2 rotate their post-SET motifs by 140° and 60°, respectively, compared to TC.
claims.source: In comparison, BC-Inh1 and BC-Inh2 rotate their post-SET motifs by 140° and 60°, respectively (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative structural comparison based on crystallographic data.

claims.claim: The post-SET motifs of BC-Inh1 and BC-Inh2 adopt more extended configurations than TC.
claims.source: Moreover, the post-SET motifs of BC-Inh1 and BC-Inh2 adopt more extended configurations with a less structured loop and a singly-kinked helix, respectively (Figures 1c and 2).
claims.evidence: This is a structural comparison based on crystallographic data.

claims.claim: The formation of Cys311 adducts likely made the key contribution to the discovery of hidden post-SET motif conformers.
claims.source: Whereas multiple factors may influence the overall conformations, the formation of Cys311 adducts likely made the key contribution to the discovery of these hidden post-SET motif conformers.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural results.

claims.claim: Crystal structures of SETD8 upon depleting native ligands were solved, obtaining structures of the SAM-SETD8 binary complex (BC-SAM) and apo-SETD8 (APO).
claims.source: To reveal additional hidden conformers that are structurally distinct from TC, we also solved crystal structures of SETD8 upon depleting native ligands and obtained structures of the SAM-SETD8 binary complex (BC-SAM) and apo-SETD8 (APO) (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplements 4 and 5, Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results.

claims.claim: BC-SAM and APO differ from TC by their distinct SET-I motifs.
claims.source: Strikingly, BC-SAM and APO differ from TC by their distinct SET-I motifs in the context of the otherwise similar SET-domain (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is a structural comparison based on crystallographic data.

claims.claim: The post-SET motif of APO structurally resembles an intermediate state between BC-Inh1 and BC-Inh2 but is distinct from those of BC-SAM and TC.
claims.source: Furthermore, the post-SET motif of APO structurally resembles an intermediate state between BC-Inh1 and BC-Inh2 but is distinct from those of BC-SAM and TC (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is a structural comparison based on crystallographic data.

claims.claim: The pre-SET motifs of the different SETD8 structures show only slightly altered configuration.
claims.source: In contrast to the structurally diverse SET-I (I1-3) and post-SET motifs (P1-4) in these structures, their pre-SET motifs show only slightly altered configuration (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is a structural comparison based on crystallographic data.

claims.claim: The differences between the SETD8 structures highlight the conformational plasticity of the SET-I and post-SET motifs.
claims.source: The differences between these structures highlight the conformational plasticity of the SET-I and post-SET motifs.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data.

claims.claim: The BC-SAM, BC-Inh1, BC-Inh2, APO, and TC structures can be classified into three distinct SET-I configurations (I1-3) and four distinct post-SET configurations (P1-4).
claims.source: The BC-SAM, BC-Inh1, BC-Inh2, APO, and TC structures can be readily classified into three distinct SET-I configurations (I1-3) and four distinct post-SET configurations (P1-4) (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is a classification of the structural data.

claims.claim: Putative 'structural chimeras' of apo-SETD8 were constructed containing orthogonal I1-3 and P1-4 in a combinatorial manner.
claims.source: We thus constructed putative 'structural chimeras' of apo-SETD8 containing orthogonal I1-3 and P1-4 in a combinatorial (3 × 4) manner (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the computational preparation of seed structures.

claims.claim: Among the twelve structural chimeras, five were crystallographically-determined conformers, four were new structurally-chimeric conformers, and three were excluded because of obvious steric clashes.
claims.source: Among the twelve structural chimeras as potential seeds for MD simulations, five were crystallographically-determined conformers (BC-Inh1, BC-Inh2, BC-SAM, TC with ligands removed, and APO), four were new structurally-chimeric conformers, and three were excluded because of obvious steric clashes (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This describes the selection of seed structures for simulations.

claims.claim: Approximately 500 × 1 µs explicit-solvent MD simulations were conducted from each seed and accumulated 5 milliseconds of aggregate data in 10 million conformational snapshots for apo-SETD8.
claims.source: Here we conducted approximately 500 × 1 µs explicit-solvent MD simulations from each seed and accumulated 5 milliseconds of aggregate data in 10 million conformational snapshots for apo-SETD8 (Appendix 1—figure 1, Supplementary file 1a).
claims.evidence: This describes the computational work performed.

claims.claim: A machine learning approach was used to identify slow degrees of freedom and structural and kinetic criteria to cluster conformational snapshots into discrete conformational states.
claims.source: To identify functionally relevant conformational states and their transitions, we built MSMs using a pipeline that employs machine learning and extensive hyperparameter optimization to identify slow degrees of freedom and structural and kinetic criteria to cluster conformational snapshots into discrete conformational states (Appendix 1—figures 2–9, Supplementary file 1b, 1c) (Husic et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This describes the computational methodology used.

claims.claim: The machine learning approach identified 24 kinetically metastable conformations (macrostates) from an optimized, cross-validated set of 100 microstates.
claims.source: This approach identified 24 kinetically metastable conformations (macrostates) from an optimized, cross-validated set of 100 microstates (Figure 4a, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1d, 1e).
claims.evidence: This is a key result from the computational analysis.

claims.claim: The 24 macrostates are remarkably diverse, spanning up to 10.5 Å Cα RMSD from APO.
claims.source: These macrostates are remarkably diverse, spanning up to 10.5 Å Cα RMSD from APO.
claims.evidence: This quantifies the structural diversity of the identified states.

claims.claim: Dimensionality reduction was used to project the landscape into 2D while preserving log inverse fluxes between states.
claims.source: To visualize the kinetic relationships between functionally important conformations, dimensionality reduction was used to project the landscape into 2D while preserving log inverse fluxes between states (Figure 4b).
claims.evidence: This describes the visualization approach used.

claims.claim: The relative populations of the macrostates were calculated, resolving rare conformational states up to 6 kT in free energy.
claims.source: The relative populations of these macrostates were also calculated, resolving rare conformational states up to 6 kT in free energy (Figures 4b and 5a).
claims.evidence: This describes a thermodynamic analysis of the states.

claims.claim: Approximately 500 × 1 µs explicit solvent MD simulations were conducted from each SAM-bound structure and accumulated 1 millisecond of aggregate data.
claims.source: With the two crystal structures of SETD8 in complex with SAM (BC-SAM and TC) as the seed conformations, we conducted ~500 × 1 µs explicit solvent MD simulations from each structure and accumulated 1 millisecond of aggregate data (2M snapshots) (Appendix 1—figure 10).
claims.evidence: This describes the computational work for SAM-bound SETD8.

claims.claim: The MSM of SAM-bound SETD8 was constructed using the same degrees of freedom as that of apo-SETD8.
claims.source: The MSM of the conformational landscape of SAM-bound SETD8 was constructed using the same degrees of freedom as that of apo-SETD8 to facilitate direct comparison of the models (Appendix 1—figures 11-13).
claims.evidence: This describes the computational approach for consistency.

claims.claim: The MSM for SAM-bound SETD8 contained 10 kinetically metastable macrostates arising from 67 microstates.
claims.source: The resulting MSM for SAM-bound SETD8 contained 10 kinetically metastable macrostates arising from 67 microstates (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1f, 1g).
claims.evidence: This is a key result from the computational analysis of SAM-bound SETD8.

claims.claim: The smaller number of metastable states identified for SAM-bound SETD8 is anticipated given that specific conformations are required for optimal interaction between SAM and SETD8's post-SET motif.
claims.source: The smaller number of metastable states identified for SAM-bound SETD8 is anticipated given that specific conformations are required for optimal interaction between SAM and SETD8's post-SET motif (Couture et al., 2005; Couture et al., 2008; Xiao et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the results supported by citations.

claims.claim: There is a large decrease in the number of slow processes seen in the SAM-bound model compared to the apo model.
claims.source: We found a large decrease in the number of slow processes seen in the SAM-bound model compared to the other two (respectively for the apo, SAM-bound, and subset of apo MSMs there are 14, 4, and 9 processes slower than 1 μs).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of the kinetic properties of the models.

claims.claim: SAM binding restricts overall conformational accessibility of SETD8.
claims.source: SAM binding thus restricts overall conformational accessibility of SETD8.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the computational analysis.

claims.claim: SAM binding dramatically alters the environment of Trp390.
claims.source: Comparison of the conformational ensembles between apo- and SAM-bound SETD8 revealed that SAM binding dramatically alters the environment of Trp390 (Figure 6a, blue sticks), the sole tryptophan residue in the catalytic domain of SETD8.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from comparing the computational models.

claims.claim: Trp390 is flexible and mainly solvent-exposed in apo-SETD8 conformational ensembles but restricted in a hydrophobic environment through SAM-mediated pi-pi stacking in SAM-bound SETD8 conformational ensembles.
claims.source: This residue is flexible and mainly solvent-exposed in apo-SETD8 conformational ensembles but restricted in a hydrophobic environment through SAM-mediated pi-pi stacking in SAM-bound SETD8 conformational ensembles (Figure 6a).
claims.evidence: This describes the structural differences in Trp390 environment between apo and SAM-bound states.

claims.claim: Environmental changes of Trp390 upon SAM binding are expected to quench fluorescence.
claims.source: Such environmental changes upon SAM binding are expected to quench fluorescence of Trp390 (Royer, 2006).
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on known biophysical principles, supported by citation.

claims.claim: SAM-dependent biphasic kinetics of fluorescence decrease was observed within 1 s with >80% of the change occurring in the fast phase.
claims.source: We observed SAM-dependent biphasic kinetics of the fluorescence decrease within 1 s with >80% of the change occurring in the fast phase (0–0.1 s) (Figure 7a).
claims.evidence: This is a direct experimental observation.

claims.claim: The major decrease in fluorescence intensity (fast-phase kinetics) is a consequence of the collective changes of Trp390 from the solvent-exposed hydrophilic environment in apo conformations to the hydrophobic environment in SAM-bound conformations.
claims.source: In the context of the conformational landscape of apo-SETD8, we interpreted the major decrease in fluorescence intensity (fast-phase kinetics) as a consequence of the collective changes of Trp390 from the solvent-exposed hydrophilic environment in apo conformations to the hydrophobic environment in SAM-bound conformations (Figure 6a).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data in the context of the computational model.

claims.claim: The minor decrease in fluorescence intensity (slow-phase kinetics) reflects the slow conformational changes of Trp390 in the SAM-bound SETD8 conformational ensembles.
claims.source: In contrast, the minor decrease in fluorescence intensity (slow-phase kinetics) reflects the slow conformational changes of Trp390 in the SAM-bound SETD8 conformational ensembles (Figure 7a).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claims.claim: Forward and reverse rate constants for the fast- and slow-phase kinetics were obtained by unsupervised global fitting to a two-step model.
claims.source: With unsupervised global fitting to this two-step model, we obtained forward and reverse rate constants for the fast- and slow-phase kinetics, which are in agreement with conventional fitting to double exponential kinetics (Johnson, 1992) (Figures 7a, b and 8a, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1h).
claims.evidence: This describes the kinetic analysis performed.

claims.claim: The k-1 value was confirmed independently by rapid-mixing stopped-flow dilution of SAM-bound SETD8.
claims.source: The k-1 value was also confirmed independently by rapid-mixing stopped-flow dilution of SAM-bound SETD8 (Agafonov et al., 2014) ('ES +E'S', Appendix 1—figure 15, Supplementary file 1h).
claims.evidence: This describes an independent experimental validation.

claims.claim: The k-1/k1 ratio of 309 ± 6 µM corresponds to the average SAM dissociation constant Kd1 of apo-SETD8 conformers.
claims.source: Here the k-1/k1 ratio (Figure 7b) of 309 ± 6 µM corresponds to the average SAM dissociation constant Kd1 of apo-SETD8 conformers, which is consistent with independently determined ITC Kd of 251 ± 16 µM (Figure 7b and c, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a calculation from kinetic data that is validated by independent ITC measurements.

claims.claim: The large k-2/k2 ratio of 30 ± 11 suggests that the second phase corresponds to a slow equilibrium between ES and E'S with minimal contribution of E'S to the overall SAM dissociation constant Kd.
claims.source: In contrast, the large k-2/k2 ratio (Figure 7b) of 30 ± 11 suggests that the second phase corresponds to a slow equilibrium between ES and E'S with minimal contribution of E'S to the overall SAM dissociation constant Kd (Figure 7c).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the kinetic data.

claims.claim: K382P mutation could better stabilize the conformational ensembles of SAM-bound SETD8 than apo-SETD8.
claims.source: We hypothesized that a proline mutation (K382P) could better stabilize the conformational ensembles of SAM-bound SETD8 than apo-SETD8 (Figures 6c and 8b).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural analysis.

claims.claim: The replacement of I293 or E292 adjacent to the α-helix with a flexible glycine should relax distortion to better stabilize SAM-bound ensembles.
claims.source: We proposed that the replacement of I293 or E292 adjacent to the α-helix with a flexible glycine should relax this distortion to better stabilize SAM-bound ensembles (Figures 6c and 8b).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural analysis.

claims.claim: K382P, I293G, and E292G variants of SETD8 showed a significant two-fold decrease of Kd,SAM.
claims.source: While exhibiting biphasic kinetics similar to that of wild-type SETD8, the stopped-flow mixing experiment revealed the three variants showed a significant two-fold decrease of Kd,SAM (Figures 7a, c and 8a).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental result validating the predictions.

claims.claim: The two-fold change of Kd,SAM mainly arises from increased SAM-binding rates k1 with relatively unchanged k-1.
claims.source: The stopped-flow data further revealed that the two-fold change of Kd,SAM mainly arises from increased SAM-binding rates k1 with relatively unchanged k-1 (Figure 8a).
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic insight from kinetic analysis.

claims.claim: Simulations of apo-SETD8 initiated from any single X-ray structure only reveal a partial conformational landscape (28–61% microstate coverage).
claims.source: The simulations of apo-SETD8 initiated from any single X-ray structure (BC-Inh1, BC-Inh2, BC-SAM, APO, or TC in Figure 1c) only reveal a partial conformational landscape (28–61% microstate coverage, Figure 9a, Supplementary file 1i).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from systematic analysis of simulation data.

claims.claim: To achieve >90% microstate coverage, at least two crystal structures—BC-SAM in combination with either BC-Inh1 or BC-Inh2—must be included.
claims.source: To achieve >90% microstate coverage, at least two crystal structures---BC-SAM in combination with either BC-Inh1 or BC-Inh2---must be included (Figure 9a).
claims.evidence: This is a finding about the requirements for comprehensive sampling.

claims.claim: The combination of I1 and I2 is sufficient to cover all 100 microstates.
claims.source: The combination of I1 and I2 is sufficient to cover all 100 microstates, arguing for the redundant character of I3.
claims.evidence: This is a finding about the importance of different structural motifs for sampling.

claims.claim: The fewer seed conformations of apo-SETD8 were employed, the more computing power was required to reach a comparable level of microstate coverage.
claims.source: For simulation time, we observed that the fewer seed conformations of apo-SETD8 were employed, the more computing power (the product between the number of simulation trajectories and the time length per trajectory) was required to reach a comparable level of microstate coverage (Figure 9e, Supplementary file 1l, 1m).
claims.evidence: This is a finding about the efficiency of sampling strategies.

claims.claim: When computing power is fixed, comparable microstate coverages of apo- and SAM-bound SETD8 can be obtained by running either multiple short trajectories or few long trajectories.
claims.source: When computing power is fixed, comparable microstate coverages of apo- and SAM-bound SETD8 can be obtained by running either multiple short trajectories or few long trajectories (Figure 10, Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding about simulation strategy.

claims.claim: The conformational landscape of apo-SETD8 can be revealed upon implementing a minimum of two seed structures (TC and BC-SAM) or 10% of the current simulation time.
claims.source: The conformational landscape of apo-SETD8 can be revealed upon implementing a minimum of two seed structures (TC and BC-SAM) or 10% of the current simulation time.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion about the minimum requirements for landscape characterization.

claims.claim: With the two seed structures (TC and BC-SAM) and sufficient simulation time, apo-SETD8 sampled 22 more microstates than SAM-bound SETD8.
claims.source: With the two seed structures (TC and BC-SAM) and sufficient simulation time, apo-SETD8 sampled 22 more microstates than SAM-bound SETD8 (89 states with 750 μs simulation versus 67 states with 850 μs simulation, Figure 9d,e), consistent with the conformational restriction of SETD8 upon SAM binding.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative comparison supporting the conclusion about SAM-induced conformational restriction.

claims.claim: It is redundant to include the four structurally-chimeric conformers because this operation contributes less than 10% of microstate coverage.
claims.source: We also noted that it is redundant to include the four structurally-chimeric conformers because this operation contributes less than 10% of microstate coverage and the comparable conformational landscape of apo-SETD8 can be generated with the subsets of seeds solely prepared from the X-ray structures (Supplementary file 1l).
claims.evidence: This is a finding about the utility of the chimeric structures.

claims.claim: The conformational landscape of apo-SETD8 takes the form of a dumbbell-like shape containing two lobes, each composed of about 12 macrostates primarily connected via a single hub-like central macrostate A11.
claims.source: When projected into two dimensions, the conformational landscape of apo-SETD8 takes the form of a dumbbell-like shape containing two lobes, each composed of about 12 macrostates primarily connected via a single hub-like central macrostate A11 (Figures 4b and 11, Supplementary file 1e).
claims.evidence: This describes the topology of the conformational landscape.

claims.claim: The hub-like macrostate A11 consists of two structurally distinct microstates with comparable populations.
claims.source: The hub-like macrostate A11 consists of two structurally distinct microstates with comparable populations (Figures 4b and 11a).
claims.evidence: This describes the composition of a key macrostate.

claims.claim: One microstate of A11 structurally resembles the conformation of APO (I3P3), while the other microstate represents a conformer with the I1P23 feature.
claims.source: One microstate structurally resembles the conformation of APO (I3P3), while the other microstate represents a conformer with the I1P23 feature for its SET-I and post-SET motifs (Figure 11b, Supplementary file 1d).
claims.evidence: This describes the structural characteristics of microstates within A11.

claims.claim: A11 is a transition-type state essential for the conformational fluxes of the macrostates between the two lobes, involved in a key step of conformational changes of the SET-I motif between {I1 ~2} and {I2 ~3}.
claims.source: Therefore, A11 is a transition-type state essential for the conformational fluxes of the macrostates between the two lobes, involved in a key step of conformational changes of the SET-I motif between {I1 ~2} and {I2 ~3}.
claims.evidence: This is a functional interpretation of the role of A11 in the landscape.

claims.claim: Conformers in the macrostates A22, A24, and A20 are structurally similar to TC and BC-SAM with slightly different but well-defined SAM-binding pockets.

results.result: Four distinct crystal structures of SETD8 were solved using covalent inhibitors (Inh1 and Inh2) and native ligand depletion (BC-SAM and APO), revealing conformational plasticity in the SET-I and post-SET motifs. These structures can be classified into three distinct SET-I configurations (I1-3) and four distinct post-SET configurations (P1-4).
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C45 provide comprehensive crystallographic evidence with detailed structural comparisons, quantitative measurements (e.g., 140° and 60° rotations), and multiple supporting figures. The data quality is documented in Table 1 with appropriate statistics. The structural classifications are well-supported by the crystallographic data.

results.result: Structural chimeras were constructed and used with crystallographic structures to seed 5 milliseconds of MD simulations for apo-SETD8. Machine learning-based MSM analysis identified 24 kinetically metastable macrostates from 100 microstates, spanning up to 10.5 Å Cα RMSD.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C53 describe a rigorous computational workflow with extensive cross-validation and hyperparameter optimization. The simulation scale (5 ms aggregate time, 10 million snapshots) is well-documented, and the machine learning approach for MSM construction is appropriately referenced and detailed in supplementary materials.

results.result: MD simulations of SAM-bound SETD8 (1 ms aggregate data) revealed 10 kinetically metastable macrostates from 67 microstates. SAM binding restricts conformational accessibility, with a large decrease in slow processes compared to apo-SETD8.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C59 provide quantitative evidence for SAM-induced conformational restriction (14 vs 4 slow processes). The use of consistent degrees of freedom for direct comparison between apo and SAM-bound states is methodologically sound. The interpretation is supported by prior structural knowledge (C57).

results.result: Stopped-flow kinetics experiments revealed biphasic SAM binding kinetics with >80% change in the fast phase. The k-1/k1 ratio of 309±6 µM corresponds to Kd1, consistent with ITC measurements (251±16 µM). The fluorescence changes reflect Trp390 environmental changes predicted by MD simulations.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C69 demonstrate strong integration of computational predictions with experimental validation. The stopped-flow data are analyzed with multiple approaches (global fitting and conventional double exponential), and key parameters are independently validated by ITC and dilution experiments. The agreement between methods strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: Rationally designed SETD8 variants (K382P, I293G, E292G) based on conformational landscape analysis showed two-fold decreased Kd,SAM, primarily through increased k1 rates, validating computational predictions.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C73 demonstrate successful structure-based design validated by experimental data. The mutations were rationally designed based on structural analysis (C70-C71), and the experimental results (C72-C73) confirm the predictions. The mechanistic insight (increased k1 with unchanged k-1) provides additional validation.

results.result: Systematic analysis revealed that simulations from single crystal structures provide only 28-61% microstate coverage. At least two structures (BC-SAM with BC-Inh1 or BC-Inh2) are required for >90% coverage. The conformational landscape can be revealed with two seed structures or 10% of the current simulation time.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C81 provide comprehensive analysis of sampling efficiency with quantitative metrics. The systematic evaluation of different seed structure combinations and simulation times is well-documented in supplementary materials. The finding that structural chimeras are redundant (C81) demonstrates thorough validation.

results.result: The apo-SETD8 conformational landscape has a dumbbell-like topology with two lobes connected by hub-like macrostate A11. SAM-bound SETD8 shows similar topology but significantly reduced complexity (10 vs 24 macrostates).
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C90 describe the network topology with detailed structural and kinetic characterization. The hub-like nature of A11 is supported by its composition of two structurally distinct microstates (C83-C84) and its role in connecting the two lobes (C85). The comparison with SAM-bound landscape is quantitatively supported.

results.result: Analysis of 20 cancer-associated SETD8 mutations revealed that 8 display neo-conformations not observed in wild-type simulations, all showing SET-I motif reorganization. Mutations A296T and H340D showed loss of methyltransferase activity. The conformational landscape approach predicted activity with 70% accuracy (14/20).
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C99 provide interesting insights into mutation effects, but the simulation time for mutants (40×1 µs each) is modest compared to wild-type (5 ms). The 70% prediction accuracy (C98) is moderate, and the authors acknowledge that some mutants (R333L, L334P) require more extensive sampling. The mechanistic interpretation (C97) is reasonable but would benefit from additional validation.

results.result: Integration of X-ray structures with 6 milliseconds of MD simulations and machine learning-based MSM construction reveals how slow conformational motions and states are relevant to SETD8 catalysis, providing molecular insight into enzymatic mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C7 and C26-C28 summarize the overall approach and findings. The integration of multiple techniques is well-executed, and the experimental validation (stopped-flow, ITC, mutant characterization) corroborates the computational models. The claim about relevance to catalysis is supported by the functional characterization of designed variants.

results.result: Conformational landscape models were experimentally explored using stopped-flow kinetics and ITC, characterizing rationally-designed variants with increased catalytic efficiency and resolving multiple timescales of conformational transitions.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C31 are supported by the detailed experimental data in C60-C73. The integration of multiple experimental techniques (stopped-flow, ITC, activity assays) provides comprehensive validation of the computational models.

results.result: Cancer-associated SETD8 mutants alter catalysis allosterically through reshaping the conformational landscape rather than directly affecting the catalytic site.
results.evaluation: Claim C32 presents an important mechanistic insight, but the evidence is primarily based on modest simulation time for mutants and moderate prediction accuracy. While the allosteric mechanism is plausible and supported by the observation that mutations are remote from active sites, more extensive sampling and additional experimental validation would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: This work represents the first definitive characterization of protein methyltransferase conformational dynamics with atomic detail. SETD8 adopts 24 and 10 metastable macrostates in apo and SAM-bound states, respectively. The SET-I motif dynamics are functionally essential for SAM binding and catalysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C106 summarize key findings and their significance. The novelty claim (C100) appears reasonable given the comprehensive nature of the study. The functional importance of SET-I dynamics (C106) is supported by the designed variants and comparison with other PKMTs (C107-C109).
